\begin{abstract}
% No citations, symbols, maths or footnotes.
A robot that knows it is lost can stop; one that trusts a wrong pose keeps driving. We therefore ask whether the failure of a localisation and mapping system is visible when the light is switched off. Two monocular systems built on 3D foundation models, VGGT-Long and MASt3R-SLAM, and \todo{the systems of the other members} run on three indoor sequences of a public ground-robot dataset with motion-capture ground truth and a LiDAR reference map. In normal light VGGT-Long has the lower trajectory error, but not always the better map. When the light switches on and off, it reports a pose for every frame and no error, yet almost all poses are more than a metre off: it tracks correctly between blackouts but joins the pieces wrongly across them. MASt3R-SLAM reports itself lost in most dark seconds, but does not recover. The underlying model marks dark images with its lowest possible confidence, but nothing marks the wrong join that follows. Code and results are public at github.com/eliasbitsch/bEARL.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Service robots move through rooms where lights are switched on and off. A camera-based system is expected to degrade in the dark; what matters for safety is whether it notices. Failure detection is an open problem of robust simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM)~\cite{cadena2016past}; under corruptions, ORB-SLAM2 reports failure where the learned DROID-SLAM and DPVO drift silently~\cite{thomas2026failure}. SLAM systems built on 3D foundation models~\cite{deng2026vggtlong,murai2025mast3rslam} have not been tested under real light changes for whether their failure is visible. On a real light on/off sequence we ask: \emph{(RQ1)} how accurate are trajectory and map in normal light, \emph{(RQ2)} how does each system fail in the dark, and \emph{(RQ3)} does the system itself report the failure? We contribute an evaluation under real illumination change with motion-capture ground truth, a silent failure localised to the joins across blackouts, with tests that rule out the dark input and the loop closure as its sole cause, and an open pipeline.

\section{State of the Art}
DUSt3R regresses dense point maps for image pairs~\cite{wang2024dust3r}; VGGT takes many images and outputs camera poses, depth and point maps in one forward pass, without bundle adjustment~\cite{wang2025vggt}. VGGT-Long joins overlapping chunks of VGGT predictions with similarity transforms (Sim(3), i.e.\ rotation, translation and scale) estimated on the shared frames and closes loops in a Sim(3) pose graph~\cite{deng2026vggtlong}. MASt3R-SLAM tracks frames against keyframes with MASt3R matches~\cite{leroy2024mast3r}, optimises a keyframe graph with loop closure and relocalises when tracking fails~\cite{murai2025mast3rslam}.
\stixSota\ \zhouSota\ \ovdiienkoSota

Robustness is often tested with synthetic perturbations, but a synthetic illumination change can reverse the ranking that real adverse conditions produce~\cite{thomas2026failure}. Under low light, MASt3R was rated robust by tracking success and trajectory error~\cite{kumar2026uavslam}, without asking whether a failure would be noticed. Introspective perception learns to predict the failures of vision systems~\cite{daftry2016introspective,rabiee2020ivslam}. VGGT's per-pixel confidence is trained as aleatoric uncertainty~\cite{wang2025vggt,kendall2017uncertainties}; VGGT reports no pose uncertainty, and its confidence predicts pose failures only partly~\cite{srinivasan2026vggtknow}. 3D foundation models produce consistent-looking geometry even for uninformative input such as noise~\cite{paul2026onescene}.

\section{Materials and Methods}
\textbf{Dataset.} M3DGR~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr} is recorded with a wheeled robot carrying an RGB-D camera (RealSense D435i, $640\times480$, 30\,Hz), a Livox MID-360 LiDAR, IMUs and wheel odometry; ground truth comes from motion capture at about 300\,Hz. We use three sequences in one $6.5\times3$\,m room: \emph{Dynamic01} (D; 175\,s, 71\,m, people walking), \emph{Sha-turn01} (S; 139\,s, 98\,m, sharp turns) and \emph{Varying-illu01} (V; 154\,s, 72\,m, light off five times for 12 to 16\,s; 46\,\% of its frames have more than 80\,\% of their pixels below grey value 20 of 255).

\textbf{Systems.} Both systems use the authors' default parameters on the RGB images and ran on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. VGGT-Long (chunks of 60 frames, overlap 30, loop closure) gets every third frame (10\,Hz), as its authors advise for dense input; MASt3R-SLAM gets all frames and exports keyframes only. \stixMethods\ \zhouMethods\ \ovdiienkoMethods

\textbf{Metrics.} The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the root mean square (RMS) of the position error~\cite{sturm2012benchmark}, computed with evo~\cite{grupp2017evo} on poses matched within 10\,ms after Umeyama alignment~\cite{umeyama1991least}, Sim(3) for monocular systems~\cite{zhang2018tutorial}; we report the median over five runs. Maps are compared with a pseudo-ground truth built by stacking MID-360 scans along the motion-capture poses, with the marker-to-LiDAR offset chosen to make the cloud as sharp as possible~\cite{levinson2010unsupervised}; after trajectory alignment and iterative closest point (ICP) refinement we report the F-score at 10\,cm~\cite{knapitsch2017tanks} up to 2.5\,m above the floor. For RQ3 we use the correct rate of OpenLORIS-Scene~\cite{shi2020openloris}: the share of the sequence time covered by a correct pose (position error $\le$ 1\,m, orientation error $\le 30^\circ$, each pose valid for at most 1\,s, the values suggested there for room-size scenes); the constant body-to-camera rotation is estimated per system on D. A failure counts as visible if the system reports it itself in its log or by relocalising; for VGGT-Long we also write out the mean depth confidence per frame without changing the algorithm.

\textbf{RQ1, accuracy.} In normal light both systems follow the ground truth (Fig.~\ref{fig:traj}). VGGT-Long has a 1.5 to 2.3 times lower ATE than MASt3R-SLAM (Tab.~\ref{tab:results}), but a lower ATE does not imply a better map: on S MASt3R-SLAM's map scores higher. The five runs of each system agree within 0.1\,mm, so their spread says nothing about robustness; only MASt3R-SLAM on V ends at 0.63 or 0.69\,m.

\textbf{RQ2, failure mode.} VGGT-Long outputs a pose for every input frame, but 97\,\% of them are more than 1\,m off; its ATE of 2.35\,m is close to the 2.39\,m that a Sim(3) alignment reaches with a constant position. Aligned per lit segment, its error is only 0.14 to 0.54\,m: it tracks correctly between blackouts and fails at joining the segments across them (Fig.~\ref{fig:timeline}), while the robot moves 3.8 to 5.3\,m in each dark phase. Neither removing the dark frames from the input (2.34\,m) nor switching off loop closure (2.35\,m; both: 2.48\,m) prevents the failure. In M3DGR, ORB-SLAM2 and ORB-SLAM3 fail on V~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr}. MASt3R-SLAM adds no keyframe in the first dark phase and reports nothing until 26.5\,s, after it ends. At the start of the second one it adds a burst of 46 keyframes on near-black images, then stops; it relocalises successfully only three times, and no keyframe follows after 132\,s. On its 26 lit keyframes its error is 0.91\,m, VGGT-Long's at the same timestamps 2.46\,m.

\textbf{RQ3, detectability.} On V, VGGT-Long has a correct rate of 0.00 and reports nothing. MASt3R-SLAM's correct rate is 0.10; on D and S its 0.53 and 0.69 are close to the caps set by its keyframe rate. Its log shows failed relocalisations in 78\,\% of the dark seconds of V, none in D and S; 16\,\% of them fall in lit seconds. VGGT's confidence has a median of 4.6 in lit frames and sits at its floor of 1.00 in dark ones (95th percentile 1.16), so the model flags the dark input. After the first blackout it is back at 4.6 in lit frames (D: 5.1), as the local geometry is right; nothing reports the wrong join.

As a check, FAST-LIO2~\cite{xu2022fastlio2} (LiDAR, IMU) reproduces the published 0.13\,m on D with 0.14\,m~\cite{zhang2025m3dgr} and reaches 0.14\,m on V, so scene and ground truth are sound. With chunk size, overlap and loop chunk size halved (16\,GB GPU, one run), VGGT-Long fails on V alike (2.23\,m).

\section{Discussion}
High aleatoric uncertainty is the expected answer to a noise-dominated image~\cite{kendall2017uncertainties}, and VGGT gives it. Between blackouts the geometry is right and the confidence rightly returns; what fails is the relative Sim(3) joining two chunks across a blackout, an uncertainty the confidence does not express, in line with its partial prediction of pose failures~\cite{srinivasan2026vggtknow}. VGGT-Long does not test whether a join is consistent: it links dark chunks with geometry from uninformative input~\cite{paul2026onescene} and, without them, chunks across 4 to 5\,m of unseen motion. Discarding bad input thus does not help; the join has to be checked, reported or bridged. MASt3R-SLAM relocalises when the share of valid matches falls below a threshold, which makes most of the darkness explicit; its keyframe burst shows that dark images can pass it too. A check on absolute confidence values, as used to filter unreliable VGGT pixels~\cite{hillemann2026vggtuncertainty}, could at least report the dark input; bridging the gaps with wheel odometry or an IMU is future work.

\textbf{Limitations.} One dataset, room and light-change sequence with five blackouts give a documented case, not a general law. MASt3R-SLAM is scored on keyframes only, which excludes its lost periods and caps its correct rate. A global Sim(3) alignment spreads a global inconsistency over all frames, hence the per-segment errors. The offset between motion-capture body and camera is not compensated, as in M3DGR.

\textbf{Conclusion.} In normal light VGGT-Long has the lower trajectory error, but not always the better map (RQ1). In the dark it fails silently, correct between blackouts and wrongly joined across them, whereas MASt3R-SLAM reports most of its loss but does not recover (RQ2). The model's confidence marks dark input, but nothing reports the wrong join once the light is back (RQ3).
